rationale: B wins because it keeps the set to the three pitches this founder can actually prove and cuts the tempting category-trend fluff. Its "The app that made women message first will now help write the message" is the cleanest tension in either set; A has the same idea, but weakens itself with "Dating apps add AI to write your opening line — and some users hate it," which turns one Bumble relaunch into a pluralized trend it cannot prove. A is strong, but B has better pitch discipline: fewer doors, less overclaim, sharper proof gates.
gaps_in_A: "Dating apps add AI to write your opening line" overstates the facts. The update gives Bumble plus user criticism of AI in dating, not a multi-company dating-app trend.
"Bumble keeps women-message-first as it hands message-writing to AI" is punchy but too hot. The facts say AI helps users write opening messages; they do not say Bumble hands message-writing to AI.
"the Dorsey/Schultz/Kalanick-adjacent storyline" is name-droppy garnish. It does not add proof, and it drags in analogies the fact block did not earn.
The broad authenticity trend and the women-message-first contrarian angle partially share the same tension. A admits the caveat, but the set still carries a little duplicate weight.
gaps_in_B: "the relaunch is the founder's first big public move since returning as CEO this year" is not in the update. It may be true, but the judge cannot credit maybes.
"Bumble's entire brand is a single authentic human gesture" overheats the grounding. Women-message-first is core; "entire brand" and "authentic" are strategic interpretation, not supplied fact.
"the market is pricing it before any post-relaunch paying-user data exists" is a fair public-market inference, but it still needs actual market reaction or valuation context before pitching.
"funding-mechanics" is the wrong story-type label for a public-company turnaround/markets angle. The substance survives, but the label is sloppy.
